blocks.text: The program does not invent separators

Each output statement contributes the characters it is given. If we display "Side" and then "North", the texts run together: SideNorth. Placing the statements on different lines in the file does not create separate lines in the output. The source code and the visible result are different representations.

A space written inside a string literal is part of its content. For example, separating two words requires at least one insertion to supply that space. You can also chain several insertions using std::cout << "Room" << " " << "Central";. Order matters, and every piece has an observable role.

blocks.text: A newline written inside the text

The escape sequence \n represents a newline inside a C++ string literal. It consists of two characters in the source code, a backslash and n, which describe a control character in the text. A line break in the source file is not the same as a newline sent to output. The position of \n determines where the next line of the message begins.

In this example, a newline separates two parts of the string literal. The output has two lines. The compiler interprets the escape sequence inside the literal; the output does not contain the backslash and n characters. For these predictions, write the visible content, including internal newlines when present; the answer field does not require a final newline.

blocks.text: Representing quotation marks and backslashes

If you need a double quotation mark as part of the message, an unescaped quotation mark would end the string literal. The notation \" represents a quotation mark included in that text. Similarly, \\ represents one backslash in the message. The character that begins an escape sequence and the resulting character have different roles: one belongs to the source-code notation, the other to the data produced.

Do not add quotation marks around the entire output answer. Include them in the answer only when the program itself produces them as content. This distinction separates the notation that delimits text from the characters that make up the text. Reading both layers will be useful later when working with paths, messages, and data.

blocks.explanation: Inside the string literal, this escape sequence represents a newline character.

blocks.text: Comments and readability

Outside a string literal, // begins a comment that continues to the end of that line. The comment communicates something to a person reading the program and is not an output statement. Inside a string literal, the same two symbols are part of its content. The role of a symbol depends on its context.

A useful comment can explain the intent or a decision that is not obvious. Repeating "displays text" next to every output statement adds little. If a comment describes a result that contradicts the code, the compiler does not resolve the contradiction: the program executes the code. That is why we also review the explanations left for others when modifying a program.

A short report experiment

Predict the lab program's output and run it. Modify the program to produce three lines: Report, East zone, and End. First change the text; then decide where the newlines should appear. You can use one insertion containing several escape sequences or several statements. Compare both versions: the organization of the code may vary, but the required output must stay the same.

Check that each line has the expected text and that the characters \n do not appear literally in the message. Write down your prediction before running the program so the observation tests a hypothesis.
Compare the lab solutions

Compare your two versions after building them. Both must display Report, East zone, and End, in that order, on three lines, without visible backslashes or additional spaces. You may include or omit a newline after End: the task does not specify that final character. A newline between the lines is required.

The first version groups the characters into one string literal; the second divides them among three statements. The characters sent to cout are the same. Splitting a statement across several lines of the source file does not, by itself, add newlines to the output.
